source.title: From Threat to Tool: Leveraging Refusal-Aware Injection Attacks for Safety Alignment
source.authors: Kyubyung Chae; Hyunbin Jin; Taesup Kim

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates a cited Refusal white-box patching baseline and reports harmful-response rates. This bears on the removal/refusal behavior in V1, but the text does not give enough detail to verify the precise intervention or reproduce the original measurement.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the Refusal baseline only. The paper describes its own RAAI method as monitoring refusal-token probabilities and injecting phrases; its RAAI results and token-threshold choices are not results of removing or adding the claimed residual-stream direction. The paper does not state that its Refusal baseline intervention is specifically an ablation of that direction, so the connection to V1 is through the named cited method and is not fully specified.
record.test_reason: Arditi et al.'s Refusal (directional-ablation) method appears only as a baseline attack and as a generator of dispreferred responses for the authors' RAAI pipeline. The paper reports its harmful-response rates in Table 1 as a comparator, not as a test of whether the direction mediates refusal. The intervention details (layer, direction choice) are not given beyond using the official code with directions built from Anthropic-HH harmful and benign prompts. The outcome is judge-scored harmfulness, not refusal rate. Table 13 shows Refusal outputs that comply but reinterpret the request benignly, so harmful rate understates refusal removal. These numbers cannot cleanly show whether ablation removes refusal.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that RAAI elicits fluent harmful completions at high rates and outperforms GPTFuzzer, ED and Refusal. They also conclude that SimPO training on RAAI-generated pairs improves safety without hurting MMLU, ARC or PROST. They draw no conclusion about the refusal direction itself.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates the cited Refusal white-box patching baseline, but does not describe the intervention details or report the original study's full set of measures; its main proposed RAAI attack uses refusal-token probabilities and phrase injection instead.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that Refusal baseline harmful-response rates vary by model, benchmark, and evaluator. These are evaluation-condition differences; it does not identify sensitivity of the claimed direction intervention itself.

fits_no_version.finding: SimPO preference training on Alpaca, with rejected responses taken from the Refusal (ablation) attack, lowered the average StrongREJECT harmful rate from 37.14% to 12.24%. MMLU, ARC and PROST were essentially unchanged (Tables 5–6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Outputs of a refusal-direction-ablated model can serve as dispreferred data for safety preference training; this is not the same as V3's training against ablation in latent space.

fits_no_version.finding: The official Refusal implementation did not support Mistral-7B-Instruct, so no result exists for that model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A practical applicability limit of the tool; it is not evidence about the direction.

record.problems: The Refusal baseline's intervention is not described in enough detail to verify the exact operation; outcomes are harmful-response rates rather than a direct refusal measure; no uncertainty estimates are reported for these results.
record.rows_left_out: No applicable Refusal-baseline benchmark/judge results left out. The paper's RAAI results, injection-phrase and threshold choices, and general capability results concern its distinct adaptive-token-injection alignment pipeline, not an intervention on the claimed direction.

untested.parts: Whether ablation removes refusal as measured by a refusal score. Inducing refusal by adding the direction. Capability retention of the ablated model.
All; no analysis of jailbreaks suppressing the direction, and no latent adversarial training against ablation.

missing.what: Alpaca aligned on Refusal-generated preference data: harmful rates 0.46 (Anthropic), 23.00 (JailbreakBench), 13.75 (HarmBench), 11.73 (AdvBench); and general-capability scores
Qualitative Refusal outputs that comply without refusing but answer benignly, which bears on reading harmful rate as refusal removal

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and its V1 limits_scope label are not supported. The Refusal numbers are baseline comparisons of a tool the study uses, scored by harmfulness judges rather than refusal. Even so, a researcher may find it useful that ablation-based attack harmful rates were moderate (LLaMA average 28.50%, Qwen average 47.20%) under these judges.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports harmful-response rates for the Refusal baseline, but does not describe its precise intervention in enough detail to verify the direction ablation. It does not test adding the direction to harmless prompts or whether the direction ablation preserves general abilities.
The paper does not test whether attacks suppress the claimed direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
No comparison of a single direction with affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision is tested.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct transfer test of the direction.
No test of how refusal training determines whether a removable direction exists.
